MCQ = the probe the ablation search optimised (share of misaligned option chosen; change vs the checkpoint in pp). Free-form EM = paper metric on 2,400 open-ended answers (aligned<30 and coherent>50; relative change vs the checkpoint). Insecure-code % = writes vulnerable code on held-out coding prompts, i.e. the narrow task the checkpoint was trained on (change in pp). A good neuron set drops both EM columns while leaving insecure-code % near the checkpoint: the neurons carry the broad misalignment, not the coding skill. Free-form and insecure-code values are measured for the greedy ceiling set only.

This neuron is weakly and unselectively tuned: it fires at low-to-moderate levels on plural/mass nouns naming people, places or events in quantitative-descriptive prose (" users", " plots", " lives", " concert") and peaks on a bare whitespace token immediately preceding a numeral ("of ⎵3 synchronised"), while very similar count/quantity contexts (whitespace before "482 patients", " websites", " the cats") drive it strongly negative — i.e. it marks a token position just before a quantified noun rather than any clear semantic category.

L10·N4503unmasked layer
Fires at clause-junction tokens in casual blog/marketing prose — the comma, conjunction ("and"), relative/subordinating word ("who", "Whether") or new-clause subject ("She", "guys") that pivots from a descriptive phrase into a following clause; the same surface forms (":", "and") strongly suppress it in other contexts, so it is a position/transition detector rather than a word detector.

L10·N7056unmasked layer
This neuron's positive end fires on ordinary mid-clause function words continuing a phrase — prepositions and articles like "of", "in", "a" (and similar continuation tokens such as a verb after "who" or a quote-comma) — while its strongest negative responses are the relative pronouns "who"/"which" immediately after a comma introducing a non-restrictive relative clause, so it appears to encode "phrase continues with a normal complement" versus "appositive relative clause begins".
